nameStory: The Cordgrass Marshhopper gets its name from its impressive jumping ability and its close association with cordgrass (Spartina) in salt marshes. Like a tiny kangaroo of the marsh, it can leap many times its own body length when disturbed. The scientific name 'spartinophila' literally means 'cordgrass-loving,' reflecting this creature's specialized habitat needs.
description: The Cordgrass Marshhopper is a small, shrimp-like crustacean that lives in the upper reaches of salt marshes rather than in water. These amphipods are about the size of a large rice grain, typically measuring 8-15mm long. They have a laterally compressed (flattened side-to-side) body that's brownish or grayish in color, helping them blend in with decaying marsh vegetation. Despite being crustaceans like lobsters and crabs, they've adapted to live on land in the moist environment of salt marshes.

idTips.label: Powerful jumping legs
idTips.description: Large, muscular hind legs that propel the animal in impressive leaps when disturbed - you'll often see them before you can examine them closely

idTips.label: Flattened body shape
idTips.description: Body compressed from side to side like a shrimp, rather than flattened top-to-bottom like many land arthropods

idTips.label: Mottled brown coloration
idTips.description: Brownish-gray color with darker mottling that perfectly matches dried cordgrass stems and marsh debris

idTips.label: Size and texture
idTips.description: About the size of a grain of rice with a smooth, somewhat translucent exoskeleton that feels firm but flexible to the touch

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of antennae, with the longer pair being about half the body length and constantly moving to sense the environment

habitat: Found exclusively in the upper edges of salt marshes where cordgrass (Spartina) meets upland areas. They live in the wrack zone - the area where storm tides deposit seaweed and debris - hiding under decaying vegetation, driftwood, and in the root systems of marsh grasses. Look for them in areas that get flooded only during the highest tides, where the substrate stays moist but not waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: Active as temperatures warm, often seen jumping away when you lift debris or walk through marsh edges. This is when they emerge from winter refugia.
seasonality.summer: Most active and easily observed during warm evenings and nights. Peak breeding season when populations are highest.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek deeper shelter in preparation for winter. Good time to find them under accumulated storm debris.
seasonality.winter: Much less active, hiding deep in marsh debris and root systems. Rarely seen unless you dig through their shelter materials on warmer days.

funFact: Despite being crustaceans that evolved from marine ancestors, Cordgrass Marshhoppers will actually drown if submerged in water for too long - they've become so adapted to semi-terrestrial life that they breathe air through modified gills and can't survive underwater like their ocean-dwelling relatives.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with terrestrial isopods (pill bugs/roly-polies) in the same habitat, but marshhoppers have the distinctive powerful jumping legs and flattened-from-the-sides body shape, while pill bugs roll into balls and are flattened top-to-bottom. Memory trick: Marshhoppers hop, pill bugs roll.
contextualKnowledge: These animals represent an fascinating evolutionary transition from sea to land - they're crustaceans that have adapted to live on land but haven't fully made the leap like terrestrial crabs. They still need the high humidity of salt marshes and represent one of the few successful attempts by marine amphipods to colonize terrestrial environments.
compareHints: As the only Uhlorchestia species regularly found in New England, compare it to other saltmarsh amphipods like Orchestia species, which tend to be larger and more robust. The Cordgrass Marshhopper is more specialized for the upper marsh zone and has proportionally longer antennae. Other marsh-dwelling amphipods are typically found closer to the water's edge and lack the powerful jumping ability.
